summary: This RFC describes the Certificate Management Protocol (CMP) for creating and managing X.509v3 certificates. It defines messages between clients and PKI components such as a Registration Authority and Certification Authority. It obsoletes RFC 4210 and RFC 9480.

eli5.summary: It is the set of forms a computer uses to ask for, renew, or cancel its digital ID with the office that issues them.

subtitle: The message protocol clients, registration authorities and certification authorities use to request, update, revoke and manage X.509 certificates.

tldr.problem: A public key infrastructure needs a standard way for devices and people to ask for certificates, renew keys, revoke certificates and learn about the PKI, over many different transports and with different levels of trust at the start.
tldr.mechanism: CMP defines a PKIMessage with a header, a body chosen from 27 message types, optional protection (a MAC or a signature) and optional extra certificates, plus rules for proof of possession, confirmation, polling and root CA key updates.
tldr.outcome: This revision adds support for certificates that hold Key Encapsulation Mechanism (KEM) public keys and prefers EnvelopedData over EncryptedValue. It obsoletes RFC 4210 and, together with RFC 9811, RFC 9480.

today: RFC 9810 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2025. It obsoletes RFC 4210 and RFC 9480 and updates RFC 5912. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What CMP Does
sections.content:
The Certificate Management Protocol (CMP) defines protocol messages for creating and managing X.509v3 certificates. It covers the interactions between client systems and PKI components such as a Registration Authority (RA) and a Certification Authority (CA).

RFC 9810 is the latest in a line of specifications. It builds on RFC 4210, which in turn changed RFC 2510, and it folds in the updates made by RFC 9480. It does not define how messages are carried. Transfers such as HTTP (RFC 9811) and CoAP (RFC 9482) are specified separately, and a transfer protocol MUST be able to deliver CMP messages reliably.

The protocol is meant to work for end entities that are humans, applications (for example IKE/IPsec) and devices such as routers or industrial control systems. The Lightweight CMP Profile (RFC 9483) is named for machine-to-machine and IoT use.
sections.eli5: CMP is a language for talking to the office that hands out digital IDs. It does not say how the letters get delivered, only what the letters say.

sections.title: PKI Entities and Operations
sections.content:
The RFC defines four kinds of party. The end entity is whoever receives the certificate. The CA is the entity named in the issuer field of the certificate, and it has final say over what a certificate contains: it may alter requested fields, for example by shortening the validity period, so every PKI entity must handle a certificate that differs from the request. An RA is an optional component that can do identity checking, request checking and similar work. When no RA is present, the CA is assumed to do the RA's job, so the protocol looks the same to the end entity. A Key Generation Authority (KGA) is also optional and generates key pairs on behalf of an end entity.

The management operations are grouped as CA establishment, end entity initialization, certification (initial registration, key pair update, certificate update, CA key pair update, cross-certification), certificate and CRL publication, key pair recovery, and revocation requests. Online messages are not the only way: for every operation there are offline methods, and the spec does not mandate online protocols.

CMP provides built-in integrity protection and authentication. It does not encrypt the whole conversation, and the RFC advises users to consider confidentiality at lower layers such as TLS, DTLS or IPsec.
sections.eli5: There is the person who needs an ID, the office that issues it, and sometimes a helper desk that checks who you are first. The office decides what the ID finally says.

sections.title: The PKIMessage
sections.content:
Every CMP message is a PKIMessage with four parts: a header, a body, optional protection and optional extraCerts (certificates that may help the recipient verify things).

The header carries the protocol version pvno, sender and recipient names, an optional messageTime, the protectionAlg, key identifiers, a transactionID, sender and recipient nonces, free text and a generalInfo list. When a sender knows nothing about itself yet, the sender field MUST hold a NULL-DN and the senderKID MUST identify the shared secret to use. Clients are RECOMMENDED to fill the transactionID with 128 bits of random data, and the senderNonce is typically 128 bits of random data that the recipient copies into the next message's recipNonce, which protects against replay.

The body is a choice of 27 message types, such as ir (initialization request), cr (certification request), kur (key update request), rr (revocation request), genm/genp (general message and response), error, certConf, and pollReq/pollRep. A response carries a status such as accepted, grantedWithMods, rejection or waiting, and failures can carry a PKIFailureInfo bit such as badPOP or badMessageCheck.

The generalInfo field has defined extensions, including ImplicitConfirm (the end entity will not send a certificate confirmation), ConfirmWaitTime, OrigPKIMessage (an RA includes the original request it modified), CertProfile and KemCiphertextInfo.
sections.eli5: Every message is an envelope with an address label, a letter, an optional seal and sometimes extra papers. The label has a number so both sides know which conversation the letter belongs to.

sections.title: Protecting Messages
sections.content:
Protection is a BIT STRING computed over the DER encoding of the header and body. It is optional, because some deployments protect messages by other means such as CMS. The RFC lists four cases for what the protection bits hold.

  • Shared secret information: a MAC using a secret established out of band, for example id-PasswordBasedMac. When the MAC needs a key longer than the hash output, the key expansion defined in the RFC MUST be used.
  • DH key pairs: when both sides have compatible Diffie-Hellman certificates, a MAC keyed from the DH result (id-DHBasedMac).
  • Signature: the sender signs the message with its signature key pair.
  • Key encapsulation: new in this document. If a sender holds a KEM key pair, the other side runs KEM encapsulation with the public key and sends the ciphertext. The key holder decapsulates it, derives a shared secret key with a KDF, and uses it for a MAC (id-KemBasedMac). The KDF context includes the static string CMP-KEM and the transactionID, and the encapsulation MUST be fresh for each PKI management operation.

An RA can forward a protected message with its own protection added, and several messages can be nested in one nested message to be forwarded as a batch.
sections.eli5: A message can be sealed with a secret handshake both sides know, with a signature only the sender can make, or with a lock that only the key owner can open.

sections.title: Getting a Certificate
sections.content:
In the basic authenticated scheme, the end entity starts out with an Initial Authentication Key and a reference value distributed out of band. It generates its own key pair, builds a certification request, protects it with that key and sends it. The RA or CA verifies the request and answers with a certification response, then the end entity sends a certificate confirmation and the RA/CA may return an optional confirmation acknowledgment. If the confirmation fails to verify, the RA/CA MUST revoke the newly issued certificate if it has been published or made available.

Proof of possession (POP) shows that the requester can use the private key matching the public key. CAs and RAs MUST enforce POP by some means. A signing key signs a value. An encryption or KEM key may be handed over for archival, or may be required to decrypt something. The preferred indirect method sends the new certificate encrypted for the end entity, which proves possession when the end entity returns the certificate hash in its confirmation, so no extra messages are needed. The direct method sends a random challenge. An end entity MUST NOT use raVerified; only an RA that has checked POP itself, or that broke the original POP by changing the request, uses it.

If the server needs time, the response status is waiting. The end entity then sends a pollReq and the server answers with the final response or a pollRep whose checkAfter field gives a time in seconds the client waits before polling again. A request sent with a PKCS #10 structure (p10cr) is allowed for legacy interoperation, but its use is strongly discouraged whenever not absolutely necessary.
sections.eli5: You get a secret code in person, fill in a form with your own key, and the office sends back your ID. You then say you got it. If you cannot show the key is really yours, the office cancels the ID.

sections.title: Root CA Key Update
sections.content:
CA keys have a finite lifetime. When a root CA changes its key pair, end entities that trust the old key need to learn the new one in a trusted way. The scheme is built on the CA protecting its new public key with its previous private key and the other way round. The operator creates up to three certificates in addition to the existing "old with old" one: newWithNew, and optionally the link certificates newWithOld and oldWithNew.

A verifier that holds only the old key retrieves the new certificates from a repository, an HTTP or FTP server, a CMP server using the root CA update general message, or out of band. It checks validity periods and the subject and issuer fields, verifies signatures with the key it already trusts, and only then stores the new trust anchor.

The RootCaKeyUpdateContent structure carries these certificates in a general response and is the replacement for the deprecated CAKeyUpdAnnContent. Unlike the old structure, it lets newWithOld and oldWithNew be omitted, depending on the needs of the end entity.
sections.eli5: When the office changes its official stamp, it uses the old stamp to vouch for the new one and the new one to vouch for the old one, so everyone can keep trusting it.

sections.title: Versions and Changes
sections.content:
The pvno field has three values: cmp1999(1), cmp2000(2) and cmp2021(3). A client that knows the server's versions MUST use the highest both support. A client that does not know them uses the highest it supports, except that cmp2021 SHOULD only be used when its syntax is needed. A server MUST answer with the same version, or with an error whose unsupportedVersion bit is set and which names a version it supports.

CMP version 3 is needed for changes to the ASN.1 syntax: EnvelopedData in place of EncryptedValue, a hashAlg field in certConf, POPOPrivKey with agreeMAC, and RootCaKeyUpdateContent in ckuann messages. Backward compatibility with CMP version 2 is kept wherever possible.

Compared with RFC 4210, the changes brought in from RFC 9480 include new extended key usages for CMP servers (id-kp-cmcCA, id-kp-cmcRA and id-kp-cmKGA), wider polling, and new general message types for CA certificates, root CA updates, certificate request templates and CRL updates. This document adds the KGA, KEM keys for POP and message protection, and clarifications moved in from RFC 4210. It also updates the ASN.1 module, and Appendix F updates Section 9 of RFC 5912.
sections.eli5: This is the newest edition of the rule book. It keeps old forms working, adds a new version number for the new forms, and adds support for a new kind of lock.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The section covers several risks. Asking for decryption can be abused, so a client MUST return decrypted values only if they match the expected content type: a valid certificate in the indirect method, or a Rand in the direct method. Revealing a private key as POP carries risk and should be used only when archival is desired and the user has agreed to trust the CA/RA. A malicious end entity could choose Diffie-Hellman parameters to attack a CA's key, so the RFC recommends that the CA generate a fresh DH key pair for each end entity.

Encrypted values use CMS EnvelopedData, which does not offer perfect forward secrecy. Where long-term security matters, CMP messages SHOULD be sent over a mechanism that does, such as TLS with suitable cipher suites. A CA should not reuse its certificate signing key for other purposes such as protecting CMP responses. Nonces and keys must come from sound random sources, and shared secrets should have entropy matching the strength of what they protect.

For KEM keys, the encapsulation function MUST be invoked afresh for each operation, and the KEM algorithm MUST be designed to be secure when its public key is used many times, such as IND-CCA2 secure ones. A trust anchor received in a CMP message MUST come from a sender authenticated with existing trust anchors and authorized by local policy. Finally, CAs that support indirect POP MUST NOT publish final certificates to Certificate Transparency logs before receiving the certConf message, though precertificates may be published.
sections.eli5: The office must make sure nobody can trick it into handing over secrets, must use good random numbers, and must not announce your new ID to the world before you have confirmed it is really yours.
